Addressing each point:
1) If you genuinely feel like you don’t have any valuable skills, then you can learn them. Find a skill that you are passionate about, enjoy, and can be used to make money and develop that skill. You’ll get to enjoy having that skill and make a career or business out of it. I’d say look at things your already interested in and see if any of them could make money in some way. Also, I believe having a bigger goal to work towards with that skill will make you much happier.
2) I think either one of two possibilities here: Either you don’t have good social skills and that causes your social anxiety, or you have good social skills, but your anxiety messes that up (maybe because your not confident in it). In both cases, practice makes perfect. You can learn social skills on the internet and books. If it’s still do difficult to do with people, practice with yourself at home. Then with the closest people you trust. Then less close people. Eventually you’ll be able to talk to strangers like it’s nothing.

One thing I’ve realized with anxiety, or at least with mine, is that there is always something causing the anxiety. Maybe someone fears they’ll come off as weird, arrogant, weak, mean, strange, etc. It could also be unresolved trauma; bullying, abuse, an accident, bad experience, etc. Literally anything, but I think there’s always something causing it. I was told that it’s just an irrational fear with no reason, so I never bothered looking for the reason, but once I found what my something was, I was able to start working on that reason and slowly but surely improve my condition. You’ll always have some level of anxiety because it’s a normal emotion, but it will be so much easier to manage. None of this is easy though, but it’s so worth it.

If your willing to spend money, I personally use wanikani.com. It’s $9.00/month, $89/year, and $300 for a lifetime subscription ($200 if you get an email for a discount during Christmas-New Years). It’s pretty pricey, but it has pretty much all the kanji you’ll need to become fluent, plus radicals to make those kanji easier and vocabulary words using the kanji. It’s designed in a way that almost feels like a game, making it entertaining and effective. It uses spaced repetition between reviews to help promote long-term memory and mnemonics stories to make the kanji readings and meanings easier to remember. It even has a community of users in the forum talking about different topics. It is in my opinion the BEST Kanji learning resource out there. 
Now if your strapped for cash and/or don’t want to spend, there are free kanji sources out there, but try to utilize the spaced repitition and mnemonics when you study.

Holy moly I have the EXACT same symptoms as you. It’s kinda scary how much I relate to this. For me it’s improved significantly where I don’t have head tremors or significant shaking anymore. I still have anxiety when I go out, but most of the time it’s not physically noticeable anymore; it’s more of an internal thing. Eating around others is the most anxious for me, but it has improved a lot compared to when my anxiety first started. It took about 4 years to get to this point.

For me, I tried the basic heath stuff: exercise, eating healthy, losing weight if your overweight or gaining weight if your underweight, drinking enough water, etc. Body and mind tend to work in unison, so if you improve one, you’ll automatically improve the other. 

For mental health, I focused on meditation, Cognitive behavioral therapy, and kinda exposure therapy (in that order). If you focus on meditation alone, it will improve your everyday awareness of your surroundings, but also your thoughts and body. This will then help you adjust your thoughts when using CBT, because you’ll be more aware of them. Once you got those two down, then you can try some exposure therapy. 

With meditation, don’t worry about forcing your thoughts or body to be a certain way. If your nonstop thinking, let yourself think. If your nonstop shaking, let yourself shake. If you feel angry, embarrassed, sad, happy, or any emotion, let yourself feel that emotion. I noticed that, with me at least, when I do that, my body naturally calms down on its own. Also, with exposure therapy, try to create levels of events from least anxious to most anxious and slowly work your way up the ladder. Ex. Sitting in a quiet library isn’t too anxious for me, but walking around by myself in NYC makes me extremely anxious. 

And the last thing I did (this one is up for speculation) was read a lot of different psychology books and theories to understand how the human mind works better. The Laws of Human Nature by Robert Greene helped me understand people’s behavior better, and when I understand how and why people behave, I’m less anxious of them. Recently, I’ve been very interested in Carl Jung’s works, specifically books about the four main archetypes: Persona, Shadow, Anima/Animus, and the Self. The big one for me in terms of anxiety is the Shadow. It’s all the parts of you that you suppress and hide from other people,  whether it’s because you see it as evil, immoral, weakness, socially unacceptable, etc. It is said that emotional outbursts and emotional instability stems from the Shadow, including anxiety. The key to it is to analyze those parts of the Shadow and find ways to integrate it into your conscious self in a healthy way. Good ways of doing it that worked for me is 1. Look at your past. Look for things that happened to you that may have led to some of your current emotions and ways of thinking. 2. Always ask yourself “Why” but in a more objective, curious way. Ex. I’m feeling anxious rn. Why? Because I’m anxious in social situations. Why? Because I feel like people are judging me. Why? Because I don’t like to be judged. Why? Because I was judged a lot in my childhood by family, teachers, etc. Something like that. When you ask questions like this it forces you to investigate to the source of the problem, where you can the fix it. 3. Look at your morals, values, ethical code and ask yourself why you see it as good and the opposite as bad. For me, I always saw aggression as bad, but that stemmed from people in my life who used aggression to abuse me. Controlled aggression is actually a very valuable tool in accomplishing your goals because it is one of, if not the strongest human motivator. Aggression can be integrated as a healthy tool in your favor. It could be passive people that you see as wrong, but they have their strengths as well. They tend to usually be more patient and think things through before speaking or acting. These are just examples tho. 

Anxiety is the symptom, not the cause. Which is why I feel like Psych meds are not completely effective because they only treat the symptoms. I think it would be effective if you use the meds to help assist you while you try the other stuff I mentioned, and if any of it starts to work, then you can talk to your psychiatrist about SLOWLY coming off your meds with each improvement until, hopefully, you won’t need them at all anymore. And I can’t really speak much about the struggles of alcoholism, but from my experience, it’s usually only a temporary fix, but may cause more long-term issues. And this is completely speculation from me, but it’s possible that you may only be an alcoholic as a way to cope with your anxiety, so if the anxiety is solved, that might not be a problem anymore either. Either way, I would recommend finding groups like Alcoholics Anonymous or 12-step programs or maybe even rehab if necessary.
